grapefruit.desc: Grapefruit, raw, pink and red, all areas
grapefruit.portion: ½ grapefruit (USDA: 0.5 fruit, 3¾ in across = 123 g)
grapefruit.offers: Half a pink or red grapefruit gives about half the daily vitamin C reference and some vitamin A, for around 50 calories. It is tart and juicy, with a pleasantly bitter edge.
grapefruit.how: Eat in segments with a spoon, add to salads with avocado or fennel, or grill with a little cinnamon.
grapefruit.cycle: Vitamin C helps your body absorb plant iron from the same meal (NIH ODS), so a piece of grapefruit alongside beans, lentils or greens is a useful pairing. No phase-specific claim is made.
grapefruit.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
grapefruit.reviewNote: The catalogue entry "grapefruit" is not specific; this is the pink and red record. White grapefruit has less vitamin A.
grapefruit.name: Grapefruit

grapes.desc: Grapes, red or green (European type, such as Thompson seedless), raw
grapes.offers: Grapes are sweet, easy-to-eat fruit with some potassium and vitamin K. A cup is mostly water and natural sugars.
grapes.how: Eat them as they are, chilled or frozen, or add halved grapes to chicken or grain salads and cheese boards.
grapes.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for grapes.
grapes.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
grapes.name: Grapes

kiwi.offers: One kiwifruit supplies about 85% of the daily vitamin C reference, along with potassium, vitamin K and a little vitamin E and fibre.
kiwi.how: Halve and scoop with a spoon, slice into yoghurt or salads, or blend into smoothies. The skin is edible if washed, though many people peel it.
kiwi.cycle: Vitamin C helps your body absorb plant iron from the same meal (NIH ODS), so a piece of kiwi alongside beans, lentils or greens is a useful pairing. No phase-specific claim is made.
kiwi.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
kiwi.name: Kiwi

papaya.offers: Papaya is a soft, sweet tropical fruit that is an excellent source of vitamin C (about 118% of the reference in a cup) with folate and potassium.
papaya.how: Scoop ripe papaya with lime juice, cube it into fruit salads and salsas, or blend it into smoothies.
papaya.cycle: Folate is a nutrient some women of childbearing age do not get enough of (NIH ODS), and a cup of papaya provides about 13% of the reference. No phase-specific claim is made.
papaya.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
papaya.name: Papaya

plum.offers: A plum is a juicy stone fruit with a little vitamin C, potassium and fibre for about 30 calories, and it is easy to carry.
plum.how: Eat whole, slice over porridge or yoghurt, roast with spices, or stew into a compote.
plum.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for plums; they are a light fruit that adds a little vitamin C and fibre.
plum.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
plum.name: Plum

pomegranate.offers: Pomegranate arils are jewel-like, tart-sweet seeds with fibre (about 3.5 g in half a cup), vitamin C and folate.
pomegranate.how: Sprinkle over salads, rice and yoghurt, or stir into dips and salsas. To open, score the skin and break it apart under water.
pomegranate.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for pomegranate; it is a source of fibre and vitamin C like other fruit.
pomegranate.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
pomegranate.name: Pomegranate

nectarine.offers: A nectarine is a smooth-skinned stone fruit with potassium and vitamin C, and a little vitamin A and fibre.
nectarine.how: Eat it ripe and whole, slice into salads and yoghurt, or grill halves for a few minutes.
nectarine.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for nectarines.
nectarine.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
nectarine.name: Nectarine

watermelon.offers: Watermelon is a fruit that is mostly water, with some vitamin C and potassium and about 46 calories in a cup.
watermelon.how: Serve chilled in cubes or wedges, blend into drinks, or pair with feta and mint in a salad.
watermelon.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for watermelon.
watermelon.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
watermelon.name: Watermelon

apricot.offers: Apricots are small, tangy-sweet fruits with vitamin A (from beta-carotene), vitamin C and potassium. Two apricots are about 34 calories.
apricot.how: Eat fresh, halve and roast with honey or spices, or chop into grain salads and porridge.
apricot.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for apricots.
apricot.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
apricot.name: Apricot

cantaloupe.offers: Cantaloupe is a sweet orange melon rich in vitamin C (about 78% of the reference in a cup) and vitamin A (about 39%), with potassium.
cantaloupe.how: Cube it for fruit salads, wrap slices with ham or cheese, or blend into a chilled soup or smoothie.
cantaloupe.cycle: Vitamin C helps your body absorb plant iron from the same meal (NIH ODS), so a piece of cantaloupe alongside beans, lentils or greens is a useful pairing. No phase-specific claim is made.
cantaloupe.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
cantaloupe.name: Cantaloupe

raspberry.offers: Raspberries are delicate, tart berries with plenty of fibre (about 8 g in a cup) and vitamin C, plus some magnesium.
raspberry.how: Eat fresh, fold into yoghurt or porridge, blend into sauces, or freeze for smoothies.
raspberry.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for raspberries; they are an easy way to add fibre and vitamin C.
raspberry.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
raspberry.name: Raspberry

peach.offers: A medium peach is a juicy, fragrant stone fruit with potassium and vitamin C for about 60 calories.
peach.how: Eat ripe and whole, slice into salads and porridge, grill halves, or bake into crumbles.
peach.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for peaches.
peach.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
peach.name: Peach

honeydew.offers: Honeydew is a pale, mild melon with vitamin C (about 41% of the reference in a cup) and potassium (about 15% of the adequate intake).
honeydew.how: Cube it into fruit salads, serve chilled with lime, or blend into drinks.
honeydew.cycle: Vitamin C helps your body absorb plant iron from the same meal (NIH ODS), so a piece of honeydew alongside beans, lentils or greens is a useful pairing. No phase-specific claim is made.
honeydew.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
honeydew.name: Honeydew melon

mandarin.offers: A mandarin is an easy-peel citrus with vitamin C (about 31% of the reference in one medium fruit) and a little potassium and fibre.
mandarin.how: Peel and eat in segments, add to salads and grain bowls, or use the juice in dressings.
mandarin.cycle: Vitamin C helps your body absorb plant iron from the same meal (NIH ODS), so a piece of mandarin alongside beans, lentils or greens is a useful pairing. No phase-specific claim is made.
mandarin.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
mandarin.name: Mandarin / tangerine

mango.offers: Mango is a sweet tropical fruit with plenty of vitamin C (about 80% of the reference in a cup), folate and some vitamin A.
mango.how: Slice or cube fresh, blend into smoothies and lassi, or add to salsas and curries. Frozen mango works well for blending.
mango.cycle: Folate is a nutrient some women of childbearing age do not get enough of (NIH ODS); a cup of mango provides about 18% of the reference. No phase-specific claim is made.
mango.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
mango.name: Mango

pineapple.offers: Pineapple is a sweet-tart tropical fruit that gives more than a day's vitamin C reference in a cup (about 105%), plus folate.
pineapple.how: Eat fresh in chunks, grill rings, or add to stir-fries, salsas and smoothies.
pineapple.cycle: Vitamin C helps your body absorb plant iron from the same meal (NIH ODS), so a piece of pineapple alongside beans, lentils or greens is a useful pairing. No phase-specific claim is made.
pineapple.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
pineapple.name: Pineapple

sweet-cherry.offers: Sweet cherries are dark, juicy stone fruit with potassium, vitamin C and about 3 g of fibre in a cup.
sweet-cherry.how: Eat fresh and pitted, freeze for a cold snack, or add to porridge, yoghurt and baking.
sweet-cherry.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for cherries.
sweet-cherry.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
sweet-cherry.name: Sweet cherry

blackberry.offers: Blackberries are deep, tart berries with a lot of fibre (about 7.6 g in a cup), vitamin C, vitamin E and vitamin K.
blackberry.how: Eat fresh, fold into yoghurt or porridge, bake into crumbles, or blend into sauces and smoothies.
blackberry.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for blackberries; they are a notable fruit source of fibre.
blackberry.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
blackberry.name: Blackberry

fig.portion: 2 medium figs (USDA: 1 medium, 2¼ in across = 50 g)
fig.offers: Fresh figs are soft, honey-sweet fruits with potassium and a little magnesium, calcium and fibre. Two medium figs are about 74 calories.
fig.how: Eat fresh and whole, halve and serve with soft cheese or yoghurt, or roast with a drizzle of honey.
fig.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for figs. Amounts here are for fresh figs; dried figs are far more concentrated.
fig.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
fig.name: Fig

pear.offers: A medium pear is a fibre-rich fruit (about 5.5 g when eaten with the skin) with a little vitamin C and potassium.
pear.how: Eat crisp and raw with the skin on, slice into salads with nuts, or poach in spiced tea or juice.
pear.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for pears.
pear.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
pear.name: Pear
